definition: Sinuous means winding and curving in a graceful, snake-like way.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word sinuous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know sinuous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: From the canyon rim the river below looked like a sinuous ribbon of silver, folding back on itself again and again.
Curved describes a single bend, while sinuous means the bending repeats, one graceful turn after another.
Serpentine is the most vivid word in the group: it insists on the image of a snake in motion, while sinuous can describe any smoothly winding shape.

Winding says a road or river bends repeatedly along its length, and it is neutral about how those bends look or feel. Sinuous is winding with grace added: smooth, continuous, snake-like curving, which is why it flatters whatever it describes.

Meandering describes a slow, lazy wandering from side to side, named for a winding river, and it hints at aimlessness -- a meandering speech loses its listeners. Sinuous keeps the repeated curves but adds grace and purpose, with nothing lazy about the line.

The old post road between the two valley towns covers nine kilometres as the crow flies, yet drivers travel twenty-six kilometres getting from one to the other.
The road never runs straight for more than a hundred metres: it swings left around a rock spur, curves right along a stream, and doubles back on itself twice near the summit.
Tour buses are banned because they cannot follow the bends.
Cyclists love the road for exactly that reason, since its sinuous course makes every kilometre a new turn.

Twenty-six kilometres of continuous bends to cover nine kilometres of straight-line distance, with no stretch straight for more than a hundred metres, is precisely the smooth, snake-like winding that sinuous describes.
descriptive; usually admiring

Sinuous is a compliment more often than not, since it suggests grace in the curving, which is why it suits rivers, dancers, and coastlines but sounds odd applied to something merely crooked or damaged.
Keep it for smooth, continuous curves: a path that turns in sharp right angles is angular or zigzagging, not sinuous.

Photographs of the Great Wall usually flatten it into a straight line, but no one who walks it remembers it that way.
The wall is sinuous: it pours along the ridgelines in smooth, continuous curves, bending with every fold of the mountains rather than cutting through them.
Its builders had no choice.
A defensive wall must hold the high ground, and the high ground of northern China goes nowhere in a straight line.
From a watchtower the result can look almost alive, a grey line curving out of one valley and into the next until haze swallows it.
Hikers say the grace is deceptive: what flows like a ribbon from a distance is a stiff climb underfoot.
